sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Srqt** ​(*serket*) — ‌Scorpions, Poison, ‌Protection of ​the ​Vulnerable · ​She who ​causes the ​throat ‌to breathe ​— belongs ​to ‌the Egyptian ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Scorpions, ​Healing, Poison". ​The ​name means ​"She who ‌causes the ​throat ‌to breathe"[^1].

​**Srqt** — ‌Serket — ​is ‌the scorpion’s ​sting turned ‌to medicine: ​the ​goddess of ‌venom and ‌its ‌cure. She ​guards the ​vulnerable — ‌children, ​the poisoned, ​the dead ‌in their ​most ​helpless passage ‌— and ​her scorpion ‌crawls ​at the ​feet of ​kings and ​coffins ‌alike, holding ‌the poison ​at bay ‌by ​its mere ​presence.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Srqt** and ​serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/serket/). The ​displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*serket* contains ‌the same ​letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or ‌special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Hieroglyphs ​as **𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐**. ​Etymologically ​it ​means "She ‌who ​causes ​the throat ‌to ​breathe"[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling ‌**Srqt** ​matches the ​conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form ‌*serket* contains ​the ‌same ​letters, so ‌no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ​transition ‌is claimed. ‌The ‌editorial ​work is ​to ‌fix ​one reviewed ​reference ‌spelling, ​preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, ​and ‌keep the ​original ​evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ‌form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ​description computed ​from ‌the ‌displayed form ‌itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**s** ​→ **S** ​— ‌Same
- ​**e** ​→ **—** ​— ‌Vowel ​not written
- ​**r** ​→ ‌**r** — ​Same
- ‌**k** ​→ **q** ‌— ​Qof
- ‌**e** → ‌**—** ​— ​Vowel not ​written
- ​**t** ‌→ **t** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name is ​**/ˈsɜːrkɛt/ ​(conventional)** ​— ‌Conventional ​reading ​— ‌Egyptian ​vocalisation ‌not ​attested.[^1]

Phoneme ‌by ​phoneme:

- ​**Sr-** ​— ​Written ​srqt; ‌the ​name ‌is usually ​explained ‌as ​“she ‌who ​causes ‌the ​throat ​to ‌breathe” ‌(s + ‌rḳ ​+ ​t).
- ‌**-q-t** ​— ​Conventionally ‌vocalised ​“Serket”; ​the ‌q is ​a ‌voiceless ​uvular ​stop.

​For ​the ‌modern ‌speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ​is: ​“SAIR-ket”

‌Kindred ‌and ‌historical ‌forms ​of ‌the ​name:

- ​**Greek** — ​Σελκίς ‌(Selkís)

​Her ​name ​is ‌a ​sentence: ​the ​scorpion-goddess as ‌the ​one ‌who ​lets ‌the ​poisoned ‌throat ‌breathe ​again. ​The final ​-t ​is ‌the ‌feminine ​ending.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Srqt** ​— Serket ‌— ‌is ​the scorpion’s ​sting ​turned to ​medicine: ​the ‌goddess of ​venom ​and its ‌cure. ​She ‌guards the ​vulnerable ‌— children, ​the ​poisoned, ​the dead ​in ​their most ‌helpless ​passage ‌— and ​her ‌scorpion crawls ​at ‌the ​feet of ‌kings ​and coffins ​alike, ‌holding ‌the poison ‌at ​bay by ​its ‌mere ​presence.[^1]

### Mistress ​of ‌Poison

Commander ​of ​the ‌scorpion’s sting; ​her ‌priests ​were the ​healers ​of venom ​bites.

### ‌Guardian ‌of the ​Dead

‌One of ​the ​four ‌goddesses protecting ‌the ‌canopic chest ‌and ​the ‌sarcophagus itself.

### ​Protector ​of Children

​Her ‌amulets ​warded nurseries; ​the ​scorpion on ‌a ​wall ​meant “no ​venom ‌enters here”.

### ​The ‌Breathing ​Throat

Her ‌name ​is a ‌cure: ‌she ​who lets ​the ​constricted throat ​of ‌the ‌stung breathe ​again.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Serket is ​a guardian more than ‌a protagonist: she ‌appears wherever protection is ​most needed, arms ​outspread over the thing ​she shields. Her ​mythic presence clusters around ​the dying god ‌— she is one ​of the four ​goddesses of the canopic ‌equipment in the Osiris ​cycle — and ‌around the threatened child, ​above all the ‌young Horus hidden in ​the Chemmis marshes.[^1]

### ​The Four Guardians of ​the Dead (Osiris ​Cycle)

When Isis wrapped ​the reassembled Osiris, ‌the four great protective ​goddesses — Isis, ‌Nephthys, Neith and Serket ​— took station ‌at the corners of ​his bier and ‌canopic chest. Serket’s scorpion ​stands for the ‌poisoned threats of the ​night that must ​be kept from the ‌god’s body; her arms ‌spread in the ‌‘Isis-knot’ gesture frame every ​royal sarcophagus hall.[^2]

### ​The Scorpion and the ‌Child Horus (Metternich ​Stela)

The great cippi ​of Horus the ‌child — the Metternich ​Stela above all ​— tell how the ‌infant god was ​stung by a scorpion ‌in the marshes ​and revived by the ​divine mother's magic. ​Serket stands within that ​cycle as the ‌power over the venom ‌itself: the sting ​belongs to her, and ‌so, therefore, does ​its antidote.

### The Scorpion ​of the King (Royal ‌Protection)

From the ‌earliest dynasties the scorpion ‌guarded the king’s ‌name — King Scorpion ​of the Predynastic ‌period took the animal ​as his emblem ​— and Serket’s image ​walked at the ‌prow and stern of ​the royal barque. ​Her presence converts the ​desert’s deadliest small ‌killer into a bodyguard.

### ​She Who Waits ​at the Head of ​the Bier (Funerary ‌Texts)

In the tomb, ​Serket and her ‌three sisters stand at ​the four sides of ‌the sarcophagus, each ​uttering protection: ‘I am ‌Serket, I encircle ‌with my protection.’ Her ​protection is specifically ​against poison and bite ​— the everyday ​killers of the Nile ‌valley made powerless ‌at the moment of ​greatest vulnerability.
